chunks.heading: What is an inverse relation?
chunks.body: An inverse relation swaps x and y in a graph. You get it by flipping (reflecting) the original graph across the diagonal line y = x.
chunks.checkText: You find a graph's inverse relation by reflecting it across...

chunks.heading: The horizontal line test
chunks.body: To check if an [[mathext1-inverse-relation|inverse relation]] is also a function, see if any horizontal line crosses the original graph more than once. If none do, the inverse is a function too.

checkOptions.text: A graph's inverse is also a function
A graph passes through the origin

chunks.heading: One-to-one vs many-to-one
chunks.body: A function is one-to-one if every horizontal line crosses it at most once. If some line crosses it more than once, the function is many-to-one instead.
chunks.checkText: A function that fails the horizontal line test is called...

chunks.heading: Writing an inverse function
chunks.body: If a function is [[mathext1-one-to-one-many-to-one|one-to-one]], its inverse is also a function, written f⁻¹(x). Don't confuse this with 1/f(x), the reciprocal — they're completely different things.

chunks.heading: Restricting a domain
chunks.body: A [[mathext1-one-to-one-many-to-one|many-to-one]] function has no inverse function. But cutting its domain down to a smaller piece can make it one-to-one, so that smaller piece does have an inverse.
chunks.checkText: Restricting a function's domain can turn it from many-to-one into...

chunks.heading: sin(x) is many-to-one
chunks.body: The graph of y = sin(x) repeats forever, so many horizontal lines cross it again and again. That makes sin(x) [[mathext1-one-to-one-many-to-one|many-to-one]] over all real numbers.
chunks.checkText: Over all real numbers, y = sin(x) is...

chunks.heading: Defining sin⁻¹(x)
chunks.body: To get an inverse for sin(x), we [[mathext1-restricting-domain|restrict its domain]] to -π/2 to π/2, where it's one-to-one. sin⁻¹(x) is the inverse of just this restricted piece.
chunks.checkText: sin⁻¹(x) is the inverse of sin(x) restricted to which interval?

chunks.heading: Domain and range of sin⁻¹(x)
chunks.body: sin⁻¹(x) takes inputs from -1 to 1, and gives outputs from -π/2 to π/2. Any input outside -1 to 1 has no answer.

chunks.heading: Defining cos⁻¹(x)
chunks.body: cos(x) is also many-to-one, so we [[mathext1-restricting-domain|restrict its domain]] to 0 to π, where it's one-to-one. cos⁻¹(x) is the inverse of just this restricted piece.
chunks.checkText: cos⁻¹(x) is the inverse of cos(x) restricted to which interval?

chunks.heading: Domain and range of cos⁻¹(x)
chunks.body: cos⁻¹(x) takes inputs from -1 to 1, and gives outputs from 0 to π. Compare this to [[mathext1-sin-inverse-domain-range|sin⁻¹(x)]], which has a different range.

chunks.heading: Defining tan⁻¹(x)
chunks.body: tan(x) is many-to-one too, so we [[mathext1-restricting-domain|restrict its domain]] to between -π/2 and π/2, excluding the endpoints, where it's one-to-one. tan⁻¹(x) is the inverse of just this piece.
chunks.checkText: tan⁻¹(x) is the inverse of tan(x) restricted to which interval?

chunks.heading: Domain and range of tan⁻¹(x)
chunks.body: tan⁻¹(x) accepts any real number as input, and always gives an output strictly between -π/2 and π/2.

chunks.heading: Always use radians
chunks.body: When working with sin⁻¹(x), cos⁻¹(x) or tan⁻¹(x), always use radian measure, not degrees. This keeps every answer consistent with the ranges you've learned.

chunks.heading: Another name: arcsin, arccos, arctan
chunks.body: arcsin(x), arccos(x) and arctan(x) mean exactly the same thing as sin⁻¹(x), cos⁻¹(x) and tan⁻¹(x). They're just two different ways of writing the same functions.
chunks.checkText: arcsin(x) means the same thing as...

chunks.heading: Reading an inverse trig answer
chunks.body: y = sin⁻¹(x) means x = sin(y), for y between -π/2 and π/2. That restriction is what picks out one correct answer from the many angles sharing that sine.
chunks.checkText: Why does the restriction on y matter when solving y = sin⁻¹(x)?

checkOptions.text: It picks out the one correct answer from many possible angles
It changes the value of x

chunks.heading: Shifting and reflecting inverse trig graphs
chunks.body: Like any other function, the graph of [[mathext1-defining-sin-inverse|sin⁻¹(x)]] can be shifted or reflected. For example, adding a number to sin⁻¹(x) shifts its graph straight up.
